claims.claim: Origen of Alexandria was an early Christian theologian and preacher who lived from approximately 185 to 253/254 CE.
Origen delivered homilies on the Psalms to his congregation in Caesarea, Palestine.
Rufinus of Aquileia selected these nine homilies for translation because, as he states in his preface, the exposition in them is 'entirely moral'—that is, free from dogmatic risks.
These homilies are among the earliest extant examples of patristic preaching on the Psalter.
The nine extant homilies consist of five on Psalm 36[37], two on Psalm 37[38], and two on Psalm 38[39].
The interpretation throughout these homilies is almost wholly moral, reflecting Origen's understanding of the 'soul' of the scriptural text.
These homilies provide a glimpse of Origen's account of scriptural meaning, outlined in De principiis 4, in pastoral practice.

In his preaching, Origen offers a vision of the Christian life as centered on the soul's continuing conversion, growth, and progress, with particular reference to and within the context of the Church.
The life of the believer is presented as one of combat and struggle with powers opposed to Christ.
Christ appears as the divine Physician who offers healing to the one wounded and ailing from sin, and as Wisdom and Word of God who instructs and educates the believer in the life of the Spirit.

These homilies reveal the substantial coherence of Origen's thought, as expressed in the more speculative De principiis and as revealed in the more elaborate, nuptial theology found in his Commentary on the Canticle.
